newsitem.title: UK: Advertising agencies lose Web business to upstarts.
newsitem.headline: Advertising agencies lose Web business to upstarts.

text.p: Advertising agencies are scrambling to learn about the Internet, but are losing business to multimedia firms hired to create Websites for consumer-related companies, a Reuters survey showed.

The survey showed 96 percent of the 30 top advertising agencies in Britain, which included global networks and local British agencies, had been responsible for putting together World Wide Websites on the Internet for clients in Britain.
Respondents said 46 percent of the top ad agencies had also put together Websites for clients outside Britain -- mostly in the United States, but also in continental Europe and Asia.

The survey, "Advertising and Marketing on the Internet", showed that while some global agencies were busy working on Websites for clients, many agencies were losing business to small, nimble multimedia companies.
Of the ad agencies that responded to the survey, 62 percent said they had only created between one and five of the Websites for clients.

Websites are electronic places on the Internet reserved by individuals or companies to communicate with others. Another 24 percent said they had helped create six to 10 Websites, three agencies helped create more than 30, while no agency said it had worked on 11 to 30 Websites.
That compared with a recent estimate by the Wall Street Journal that companies worldwide were creating a staggering 60,000 new corporate Websites every month.

People and companies are using websites to communicate about almost anything, including selling things to advising investors to chatting with Internet users. Some companies that responded to a related Reuters survey said they dealt only with multimedia companies to create Websites and avoided ad agencies which they felt were ill-equipped to work on Internet-related projects.
Jeremy Silver, vice president for interactive media at EMI International, a part of EMI Group Plc music publisher, delivered a harsh verdict on ad agencies and the Internet.
"Stay clear of ad agencies if you want a good Website. They don't understand the Internet -- which is bizarre, since you would expect them to be at the cutting edge," he told Reuters.
"It's a real indictment of the ad industry. There's a real lack of strategic thinking in the ad industry," he said.
Some company officials told Reuters ad agencies were still recovering from massive layoffs triggered by the recession and lacked the staff to gear up for Website-related business.
Many companies said they were unhappy with the outside group -- whether an ad agency or multimedia company -- that created their Websites.
Only 43 percent of companies that responded to the survey said they would use the same outside agency or company again, 17 percent said they would not and the remainder were unsure.
But some companies had glowing reports about their ad agencies and Websites.
IM, which has about 50 different Websites and offices in 250 countries, and Guinness Plc, said it was happy with Ogilvy & Mather, the ad agency they had used for their Websites.
Procter & Gamble, the world's biggest advertiser, praised Grey Advertising, which coordinated the creation of P&G's dozen-odd Websites.
Tony Evertts, the head of new media at TBWA advertising agency, said clients were better off hiring agencies than multimedia companies.
"We know more about media than Website companies. And we're not more expensive than the Web companies," he told Reuters.

But while agencies like Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising and J.Walter Thompson had created new divisions to work on Websites and other new media ventures, many agencies seemed lost and confused when asked by Reuters whether they created Websites.

When ad agencies were asked whether they had hired full-time employees in the last 12 months to work on Websites in Britain, 52 percent of respondents said "yes" and 48 percent said "no". The vast majority of ad agencies that took on new staff for Websites only hired between one and 10 people.
Ad agencies said they farmed out to freelancers or consultants most of the Website creation requested by clients.
Only one-quarter of the ad agencies surveyed said they planned to hire people over the next year to work on Websites, while more than two-thirds said they would not.
